parts.visual:
Pitch A: 'We make a faster database using C++.' Pitch B: 'The old data system was designed for the 1990s and is currently crashing the modern web. We are building the nervous system for the AI revolution.' Pitch A gets 100 users. Pitch B raises $50 Million and gets on the cover of Forbes.

The Narrative:
1. Features vs. Worldview: Great startups do not sell software features; they sell a fundamental shift in how the world operates. The 'Strategic Narrative' frames the startup not as a tool, but as the inevitable winner of a historical transition.
2. The Enemy: Every great narrative requires a villain. The villain isn't always a competitor; it is usually an outdated concept, an inefficient system, or a massive, lazy monopoly.
parts.audio: A strategic narrative is a story that makes the status quo look completely unacceptable. You have to convince the world that living without your product is not just inconvenient, but morally and technologically backward.

questions.question: When Salesforce launched, their CEO staged a fake protest outside a competitor's conference with signs saying 'NO SOFTWARE'. What was the strategic narrative?
options: The Old World vs. The New World. He framed traditional, CD-ROM installed software as the villain (expensive, slow, dead). He framed Salesforce (cloud computing) as the inevitable, liberating future. He didn't sell features; he sold a revolution.
questions.correct_answer: The Old World vs. The New World. He framed traditional, CD-ROM installed software as the villain (expensive, slow, dead). He framed Salesforce (cloud computing) as the inevitable, liberating future. He didn't sell features; he sold a revolution.
questions.explanation: If you define the enemy perfectly, you automatically define yourself as the hero.

questions.question: Listen to the PR expert explaining how to pitch to journalists. What must the founder explain first?
questions.tts_text: If you start by talking about your app, I will hang up the phone. You must start by explaining a massive, terrifying shift happening in the world right now. Then, you introduce your company as the only logical response to that shift.
options: The 'Why Now?' The narrative must create urgency. You must convince the world that a massive technological or cultural tsunami is happening at this exact second, and your startup is the only lifeboat.
questions.correct_answer: The 'Why Now?' The narrative must create urgency. You must convince the world that a massive technological or cultural tsunami is happening at this exact second, and your startup is the only lifeboat.
questions.explanation: A great product launched at the wrong time is irrelevant.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'Positioning' and 'Messaging'?
options: They are the exact same thing.

Positioning is the foundation (Who is this for? Who are we fighting? Why are we different?). Messaging is the exact words you put on the website to explain the positioning. If the positioning is wrong, the messaging will sound like garbage.
Positioning is for physical products only.
questions.correct_answer: Positioning is the foundation (Who is this for? Who are we fighting? Why are we different?). Messaging is the exact words you put on the website to explain the positioning. If the positioning is wrong, the messaging will sound like garbage.
questions.explanation: Positioning is the strategy. Messaging is the tactic.

questions.question: Why is 'We are like Uber, but for Dog Walking' a weak strategic narrative for a Series B company?
options: It is derivative. 'X for Y' works for a Seed round to quickly explain the mechanics. But a mature company needs an original worldview. If your identity relies entirely on comparing yourself to another company, you are not a visionary; you are a copycat.
questions.correct_answer: It is derivative. 'X for Y' works for a Seed round to quickly explain the mechanics. But a mature company needs an original worldview. If your identity relies entirely on comparing yourself to another company, you are not a visionary; you are a copycat.
questions.explanation: Leaders invent analogies. Followers use them.

questions.explanation: People don't buy code; they buy a better future.
